chapters.title: Chapter 3: Working Capital Policy and Requirement

lessons.title: Aggressive, Conservative or Moderate: Choosing a Working Capital Policy

children.text: Two identical fastener units in Ludhiana buy the same steel, run the same machines and sell to the same customers. One holds 45 days of stock and gives 60 days of credit. The other holds 20 days of stock and insists on 30 days. The first never disappoints a customer and never earns much. The second earns well and occasionally loses an order because a size was out of stock.
Neither is wrong. Each has chosen a working capital policy, and this lesson is about making that choice deliberately instead of drifting into one.
Policy Has Two Separate Questions
Almost every confused discussion about working capital policy comes from mixing up two decisions that are made separately and have different consequences.

columns.label: How much to hold
points: How many days of inventory, and what safety stock
What credit terms to offer, and to whom
How much cash to keep as a buffer
This decides the size of current assets
Trade-off: service level and sales against return on capital

columns.label: How to fund it
points: How much comes from cash credit and short-term borrowing
How much from long-term loans and the company's own funds
This decides the mix of financing, not the size
Trade-off: interest cost against refinancing risk

children.text: A business can be lean on the first question and conservative on the second, or any other combination. Treat them as one decision and you will keep arguing about the wrong thing.
Question One: How Much to Hold

Bharat Fasteners Ltd has sales of ₹200 crore, operating profit of ₹24 crore and fixed assets of ₹60 crore. Everything about its operations is fixed except how much it chooses to carry in current assets. Watch what that alone does to
return on capital employed

markDefs.definition: Return on capital employed. Operating profit divided by the capital funding the business, which includes working capital.

body.caption: Same profit, three current asset policies (₹ crore)

body.title: Return on capital employed under three current asset policies

children.text: The operating business is identical in all three columns. Holding current assets at 35% of sales instead of 20% costs 5.5 percentage points of ROCE, purely because ₹30 crore more capital is parked in stock, receivables and cash.

body.caption: Working capital sits in the denominator, so every rupee held there dilutes the return

body.text: This table is why finance teams push for lean working capital and why operations and sales teams resist. Both are right. The table shows only the cost of holding current assets, never the cost of not holding them.

children.text: Now add that missing half. Suppose the lean policy causes stockouts that cost 4% of sales, that is ₹8 crore of revenue at a 12% margin, or ₹0.96 crore of profit. ROCE under the lean policy falls from 24% to 23%, still ahead of the moderate policy. If the stockouts also cost you a long-standing customer, the arithmetic changes completely and no table can capture it.

body.title: Test the trade-off yourself
body.prompt: Using the same Bharat Fasteners figures, sales of ₹200 crore, operating profit of ₹24 crore and fixed assets of ₹60 crore, what is the ROCE if current assets are held at 32% of sales? Answer as a percentage to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Current assets are 32% of ₹200 crore, which is ₹64 crore. Capital employed is ₹60 crore plus ₹64 crore, which is ₹124 crore. ROCE is ₹24 crore divided by that, or 19.4%. Every extra ₹4 crore of working capital costs roughly half a percentage point of return here.

children.text: Question Two: How to Fund It

Take the moderate policy, with ₹56 crore of current assets to fund. Assume short-term bank finance costs 9.5% and long-term funds cost 12%, which is the usual shape in India, where cash credit prices below term debt.

body.caption: Three financing mixes for the same ₹56 crore (₹ crore)

body.title: Matched financing: where the funding comes from (₹ crore)

children.text: The aggressive mix saves ₹0.56 crore a year, about ₹56 lakh, against the conservative one. That is real money, and it is also the entire case for aggressive financing. What it buys you is exposure.

body.title: Why cheap short-term money is riskier than it looks in India

children.text: A cash credit limit is a
demand facility

. The bank can reduce or withdraw it, and the limit comes up for renewal every year. A business that funds a permanent need with a facility that can be pulled has a structural mismatch, not just a cheaper interest line.

markDefs.definition: A facility the bank can call back or reduce at short notice, regardless of whether the borrower has defaulted.

children.text: Second, the amount you can actually draw is not the sanctioned limit. It is the
drawing power

, recalculated every month from the stock and book debt statement you submit, after deducting a margin and usually excluding receivables older than 90 days. Exactly when the business is struggling, with stock unsold and collections slow, the drawing power shrinks. The facility is smallest when the need is greatest.

markDefs.definition: The borrowing limit actually available in a month, calculated from the stock and receivables declared to the bank after applying a margin.

children.text: Third, rates move. Most working capital limits in India are linked to an external benchmark such as the repo rate, so the cost resets as policy rates change, while a term loan taken at a fixed spread on a longer tenor is more predictable.
Chapter 6 covers drawing power, margins and stock statements in detail.

body.title: Pick the policy for the business
body.question: A manufacturer of school uniforms sells 70% of its annual volume between April and July. Which financing policy fits best?
options: Fund the entire peak requirement with long-term debt, so nothing has to be renewed
Fund the year-round base requirement with long-term funds and the seasonal peak with short-term bank finance
Fund everything with cash credit, since it is the cheapest available money
Avoid all borrowing and hold the peak requirement in cash through the year
body.explanation: This is the matching principle. The portion of working capital that never goes away should be funded with long-term money that cannot be withdrawn, while the seasonal bulge is funded with short-term finance that can be drawn in April and repaid by August. Funding the peak entirely long-term leaves expensive money idle for eight months; funding the base with cash credit creates a permanent dependence on a facility that is repayable on demand.

body.label: The matching principle
body.value: Fund permanent needs with permanent money
body.context: Match the life of the asset to the life of the funding. The next lesson separates permanent from temporary working capital and shows how to fund each.

children.text: Putting the Two Choices Together

stats.label: Lean and aggressive
stats.context: Works with stable demand, reliable suppliers and disciplined collections

stats.label: Moderate and matched
stats.context: Base need funded long-term, seasonal peak funded short-term

stats.label: Cushioned and conservative
stats.context: Suits volatile demand, long supply chains or concentrated customers

children.text: The right combination depends on four things: how predictable your demand is, how reliable your supply chain is, how concentrated your customers are, and how much undrawn bank limit you have as a fallback. A business selling to three large original equipment manufacturers on 90-day terms cannot afford the same policy as one selling to 400 dealers against advance payment.

body.title: The matching rule
body.textWithBlank: Under the matching principle, permanent working capital should be funded with ___ term sources, while seasonal peaks are funded with short-term finance.
body.explanation: Matching the tenor of the funding to the life of the need is the core of financing policy. Permanent needs funded with demand facilities create a structural risk, however cheap the interest looks.

body.title: Setting policy for a growing business
body.scenario: You advise a Coimbatore pump manufacturer with ₹150 crore of sales growing at 25% a year. It sells to 120 dealers on 45-day terms, holds 60 days of finished stock across 40 models, and funds everything through a ₹40 crore cash credit limit that is 90% drawn. The promoter refuses to raise equity and wants to keep growing at the same rate. Margins are 14%.
body.prompt: What working capital policy would you recommend, on both questions, and what would you do first?
body.modelAnswer:
Start by naming the real problem. The business is running a moderate holding policy funded almost entirely through a demand facility that is nearly exhausted. At 25% growth, working capital needs to grow roughly in step, so it will need about ₹10 crore more funding next year at current ratios. There is ₹4 crore of headroom. The policy is not aggressive, it is unfunded.

On the holding question, go leaner but selectively. Forty models across 60 days of stock almost certainly hides a long tail: apply an ABC split and hold deep stock only on the models that drive most of the volume, cutting perhaps 10 to 15 days on the rest. On credit, keep 45 days for dealers who pay on time and tighten the slowest decile, with a small early-payment discount to pull collections forward.

On the financing question, stop funding permanent needs with cash credit. The base level of working capital that never goes away should move to a working capital demand loan or a term loan, which cannot be withdrawn on demand, leaving the cash credit limit free to absorb seasonal swings. Ask the bank for an enhancement based on the growth projection, and expect to bring margin money for it.

What to do first: build the projection. Take next year's planned sales, apply the current cycle in days, and show the promoter the rupee funding gap. That number, not an argument about policy, is what will settle whether growth at 25% is fundable without new capital. The next two lessons build exactly that estimate.

body.title: Set a working capital policy deliberately
steps: Write down your current position first: current assets as a percentage of sales, and the split of funding between short-term and long-term sources.
Compare that percentage with two or three comparable listed companies over five years, using screener.in.
Assess demand volatility, supply reliability and customer concentration, since these decide how much cushion the business actually needs.
Set a target range for inventory days and receivable days by category or customer segment, not a single company-wide number.
Identify the permanent portion of working capital that never goes away, and check that it is funded by long-term sources.
Keep a defined share of the cash credit limit undrawn as standby liquidity, and treat it as a policy rule rather than a coincidence.
Review the policy annually against actuals, and after any large change in customer mix, product range or growth rate.

body.text: Working capital policy is not a finance department preference. It is a statement about how much return you are willing to give up to be certain you can serve a customer and pay a bill.

body.label: Benchmark a policy against listed peers
body.description: Working capital as a percentage of sales, read across five years for three peers, tells you the policy band your industry actually operates in. DMart is a useful extreme: a lean holding policy funded almost entirely from operations.

points: Working capital policy has two separate questions: how much to hold in current assets, and how much of it to fund with short-term money.
Holding more current assets lowers risk and lowers return, because working capital sits in the denominator of ROCE.
In this example, moving from a lean to a cushioned holding policy cost 5.5 percentage points of ROCE on identical operations.
Lean policies carry costs that ratios do not show, such as stockouts and lost customers, so the trade-off must be judged commercially.
Short-term funding is cheaper but riskier in India, because cash credit is repayable on demand and drawing power shrinks exactly when the business is under strain.
The matching principle is the default: fund permanent working capital with long-term sources and seasonal peaks with short-term finance.
The right policy depends on demand volatility, supply reliability, customer concentration and how much undrawn limit is available as a fallback.
